Gastroenterology · published research

Microbiota

Summary of the Evidence

Twenty-five relevant publications are listed after two candidate reports that did not test PBM were excluded. The literature spans human reports, animal studies, and reviews. Three records use indirect or combined light protocols, and some publications reuse participants or synthesize the same underlying studies. The total is therefore not a count of independent treatment trials.

A 2025 systematic review of abdominal PBM included nine studies, five human and four animal. The authors described the evidence as preliminary because samples were small, protocols and treatment sites varied, and few human studies were sham-controlled. The review combined microbiome, metabolic, and neurobehavioral outcomes, so it does not provide a pooled estimate for microbiome change alone (Guimarães et al. 2025).

Human and clinical evidence

A 2022 retrospective analysis reported stool microbiome changes after a 12-week PBM programme in 12 people with Parkinson's disease. It reanalysed samples from a previously reported treatment cohort, so it adds a microbiome outcome rather than a new treatment group (Bicknell et al. 2022).

A separate case report followed one person receiving radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and PBM. Some microbial diversity measures and taxa changed over time, but the combined treatment and single-person timeline cannot identify which factor caused the changes (Bicknell et al. 2022).

A four-person oral-mucositis pilot reported changes in selected oral bacteria alongside inflammatory markers. In a later six-person randomized split-mouth study during orthodontic retention, PBM did not significantly change overall plaque-community structure. These oral findings do not establish effects on gut microbes (Zanotta et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2026).

A five-year case series analysed stool samples from six Parkinson participants who continued the earlier treatment programme. Microbial evenness and composition changed over time, but the small uncontrolled follow-up cannot separate PBM from diet, medication, ageing, or other influences. These participants came from the earlier cohort (Bicknell et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

In mice, repeated 808-nm abdominal irradiation changed fecal microbial diversity and increased Allobaculum, while the tested red-light schedule did not produce the same result (Bicknell et al. 2019). A type 2 diabetes rat study found changes in several gut bacterial genera after one session of dual-wavelength light delivered inside the duodenum (Min et al. 2022).

In an Alzheimer's disease mouse model, 810-nm gut-targeted PBM changed microbial metabolites and short-chain-fatty-acid-producing bacteria, while transcranial treatment produced minimal microbiome change (Cao et al. 2025). In a separate colitis model, 830-nm PBM increased microbial richness and altered composition while inflammatory and disease-activity measures also improved. These animal results do not show that microbial changes caused the disease-related improvements (Maeng et al. 2026).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from abdominal 660-nm red and 808-nm near-infrared laser exposure in mice to repeated 904-nm abdominal treatment in a Parkinson cohort. Other reports used 970-nm intraoral light for oral mucositis, 940-nm intraoral treatment during orthodontic retention, or light delivered directly into the duodenum. Recent animal models tested 810-nm gut-targeted or 830-nm abdominal treatment. Doses, target sites, timing, microbial sampling, and sequencing methods differ. Oral, gut, and skin microbiomes are not interchangeable, and no head-to-head study establishes an optimal wavelength or schedule.

Interpretation

PBM has coincided with measurable microbiome shifts in some human and animal settings, while a small oral split-mouth trial found no significant change in overall community structure. The direction and meaning of a shift depend on the body site, protocol, and taxa measured. Current evidence does not show that a microbiome change itself caused improved health or disease outcomes.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Low for short-term microbiome composition changes in small human cohortsVery low for clinical benefit caused by microbiome changes

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Small human reports include a retrospective microbiome analysis and a five-year follow-up of participants from the same Parkinson treatment programme, as well as a single case and small oral studies. A 2025 review found small samples, varied protocols and combined treatment sites, with few sham-controlled human trials. This supports low certainty about short-term composition changes and very low certainty that such changes cause clinical benefit (Bicknell et al. 2022; Bicknell et al. 2026; Guimarães et al. 2025).
